title: The Gebir; a Spanish Romance, Poetical, in Four Books
alternative_titles: Gebir
description: The author's first published poem, a four-book romance in Spenserian stanzas drawn from a supposed Moorish-Spanish source about an infant heir of Spain. The story mixes dynastic exile, enchanted river-gods, and a quest for water that turns out to be a quest for the poet's own blood. It is at once a late-romantic allegory and a deliberate archaism, and it established the dense, allusive manner kept for the rest of its author's career.
plot_or_argument: Gebir, infant son of the murdered King Alphonso of Spain, is saved from his uncle's slaughter by being laid in a brazen cradle upon the waters and nursed in secret among goatherds. Grown unknown to himself, he loves his sister Gwendolin without knowing her kinship, and marches to war against the giant Dan and the Sorayzan host. A drought afflicts his army, and Gebir descends through caves of the earth to seek water from the river-gods of the Guadalete and the Genal. There he must pass the guard of the serpent Tondalu and is shown, in visionary genealogies of Spain, his own destiny. He learns that the promised stream can flow only from his own wounded heart; he slays Tondalu, is himself destroyed in the effort of the victory, and his life-giving water rises to relieve the host.
narrative_structure: Continuous four-book narrative romance in Spenserian stanzas, with prophetic visions and set-piece descents interrupting the linear plot; the middle books form a katabasis framed by the two outer war narratives.
principal_characters: Gebir; Gwendolin; Alphonso; Dan; Tondalu; the river-spirits Guadalete and Genal
literary_form: Romance in verse: an English Spenserian romance that revives allegorical machinery, enchanted guardians and genealogical prophecy from The Faerie Queene while treating the matter as symbolic rather than narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Spenserian stanzas (nine lines, ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the closing alexandrine; archaic diction and inverted syntax throughout.
historical_context: Written in the first flush of the 1790s romancing reaction and published as its author left Oxford; its withdrawn first issue made it a bibliographical rarity for a generation, and its Jacobean archaism answers the decade's taste for romance and for Spenserian revival.
literary_significance: A landmark of the romancing reaction of the 1790s, and one of the earliest English poems to treat dynastic exile and thirst as a private mythology; Swinburne and later Pre-Raphaelite readers made it the keystone of its author's reputation as a poet rather than as a prose stylist.
attribution_notes: Published without the author's name; Its author acknowledged it in later life, and the 1798 date rests on bibliographical evidence rather than a dated title page.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1798; the volume carries no author's name and the imprint is that of a privately funded issue, of which the author bought up and suppressed the unsold copies almost immediately.

title: Letters written during a short residence in Spain and Portugal
alternative_titles: Letters written during a short residence in Spain and Portugal, in 1795 and 1796
description: The author's Iberian travel letters, worked up from notes taken during his walking tour of northern Spain with John Favero in 1795-96. The volume combines picturesque description of coast, mountain and monastery with antiquarian discussion, political observation and an open sympathy with the Spanish and Portuguese poor. It is the founding text of his career as a traveller-author and the source of the Iberian colour he later used in verse.
plot_or_argument: The letters narrate a pedestrian tour from Lisbon through the valleys of Asturias and Old Castile and back, pausing at mines, cathedrals, baths and fishing villages. The writer estimates populations, agriculture and monastic wealth, and argues that Iberian poverty is the product of misgovernment rather than of climate or national character. Antiquarian detours on early Spanish poetry, Moorish remains and local institutions are woven into the route. The closing letters weigh the prospects of reform in the peninsula and the consequences of the war with Revolutionary France.
narrative_structure: Epistolary sequence in dated letters following a geographical itinerary; description, disquisition and correspondence with friends alternate without a sustained argumentative thread.
literary_form: Travel letters / topographical epistle: a pedestrian tour narrative in the manner of Young and Arber, enlarged with antiquarian essay and political economy.
historical_context: Written by a twenty-two-year-old former Jacobin just after the French Revolutionary War began on the peninsula, the book refracts its author's desertion of radical politics through a sympathetic but Protestant, anti-monastic view of Catholic Spain.
literary_significance: It fixed the Iberian setting later exploited in the romances of the same author, and it is a primary document of 1790s pedestrian tourism and of the romantic picturesque applied to the peninsula.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1797, issued in quarto form with engravings, and written up from the 1795 tour; a second edition followed quickly as the war with Spain made Iberian information a marketable commodity.

title: Letters from England
alternative_titles: Letters from England: by Don Manuel Alvarez Espriella
description: The author's most influential prose work: a long series of letters on England written in English but affected to be the observations of a fictitious Spanish refugee correspondent. The persona lets the writer praise and blame his own country as though seeing it for the first time, in a manner consciously modelled on Addison's Spectator papers. The range is enormous - lakes and manufactories, Dissent and the slave trade, duelling, the theatre, the poor laws.
plot_or_argument: The personating correspondent, a South American of Spanish descent resident in England, writes to friends in Philadelphia and Lisbon about the country he has settled in. He tours the Lake District, the Scottish border, the industrial towns and London, and uses each place to draw out an argument about national character, religion, commerce or liberty. His foreign eye permits both extravagant praise of English institutions and satiric attack on Methodism, political corruption and the treatment of the poor. Alongside the travel letters are essays on the slave trade, on the Roman Catholic Question, and on literature and the drama, and a running quarrel with the Review journals.
narrative_structure: Epistolary periodical sequence: numbered letters of unequal length gathered into volumes, loosely organised by journey and by subject rather than by argument.
principal_characters: the personating Spanish-refugee correspondent; his Philadelphia and Lisbon addressees
literary_form: Periodical essay in epistolary form, a deliberate continuation of the Spectator paper and of the travel letter, with embedded disquisition and satire.
historical_context: The letters first appeared in the Anti-Jacobin Review from 1804 and were collected in the three volumes of 1806-08, when its author had broken with his early radicalism and was building a Tory public identity; the Spanish mask answers the decade's war with Spain and its hunger for picturesque domestic travel.
literary_significance: It made its author famous to a broad reading public as the poet of the Lakes, supplied the earliest substantial romantic prose celebration of the Lake District, and gave later guide-book writers and travellers the model of the foreign persona criticising England.
attribution_notes: Published under a pseudonymous by-line personating a Spanish refugee correspondent, a persona properly recorded with the author rather than in this work record; the authorship was an open secret and the by-line was dropped in later collected printings.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in three volumes in 1807, the first two volumes appearing together and the third following, with several of the letters reprinted from the Anti-Jacobin Review where they had appeared under the same by-line; a fourth volume was added in later editions and the whole was reprinted several times in the nineteenth century.

title: The Chronicle of the Cid
alternative_titles: The Chronicle of the Cid, translated from the Spanish
description: The author's prose translation of the medieval Castilian chronicle of Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar, made from the Spanish edition of the royal academy and addressed to John Hookham Frere. It is both a scholarly performance, with a long prefatory dissertation on the poem's date, authorship and metrics, and a piece of propaganda for chivalric example in the age of Napoleon. The volume is a landmark of British Hispanism.
plot_or_argument: The chronicle follows the Cid from his banishment from Castile through his campaigns as an independent leader in the marches of al-Andalus to the conquest of Valencia and the famous judicial duel of the Cide's daughters. Its episodes praise loyalty, courage and liberality, and its ending restores the Cid to royal favour through alliance with the houses of Navarre and Barcelona. The translator's dissertation argues for the antiquity and the oral-professional origins of the Castilian epic, and compares it with the French chansons and with the Spanish romances.
narrative_structure: Prose translation of a continuous chronicle, preceded by a substantial editorial dissertation; the narrative proceeds in campaign episodes with genealogical and formulaic recurrences.
principal_characters: The Cid (Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar); Ximena; King Alfonso; the Counts of Carrion; King Motamid of Seville
literary_form: Translation of an epic chronicle, with critical dissertation; a chivalric and national heroic narrative rendered into English prose.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, with occasional verse and stanzaic quotations from the Spanish romances.
historical_context: Published at the opening of the Peninsular War, when Spain became an object of British popular sympathy; The author's own friendship with Spanish scholars in London and his interest in the Cid as a model of Christian knighthood drove the volume.
literary_significance: The first widely read English version of the Castilian national epic, it supplied the Cid legend to the whole nineteenth-century British romance revival, and its dissertation anticipates modern scholarship on the Cantar de mio Cid.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1808, printed in an edition paid for by John Hookham Frere and circulated privately before general sale, with a dedication to Frere and engravings after Spanish originals.

title: A Tale of Paraguay
description: The author's last completed long narrative poem, a romance of the Jesuit reductions of Paraguay, published in the volume that also contained his Vision of Judgement and other short pieces. It deliberately abandons the machinery and the exotic theatres of the earlier metrical tales for a quieter, domestic and more humane story of love across the boundaries of race and creed. The poem is a summary of its author's late romantic practice: courteous, elegiac, and sceptical of conquest.
plot_or_argument: The tale is laid in the Guarani mission towns of Paraguay and turns on the affection of a Spanish settler for a daughter of the converted Indians, and on the trial their union undergoes from the greed of the colonists and from the slave-hunting raids of the Paulistas upon the reductions. The poem gives the missions a social reality - their agriculture, their music, their government by the Jesuit fathers - and sets against it the avarice of those who would divide the Indians among themselves. Persecution, displacement and separation test the lovers, and a providential close restores what rapacity had nearly destroyed. Interpolated songs and lyric apostrophes mark the crises of the story, and the poet's comment on the usage of the Indians grows plainer as the narrative proceeds.
narrative_structure: Continuous narrative poem in cantos, interrupted by inserted songs and lyric addresses and by a first-person editorial comment that grows stronger as the tale approaches its close.
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse: a domestic romantic narrative in the line of his earlier tales, reduced in scope and raised in moral seriousness.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly blank verse with rhymed stanzas and interpolated lyric songs; a softer, more conversational movement than the earlier metrical tales.
historical_context: Written after its author's accession to the laureateship in 1813 and during his residence at Green Hill, Wimbledon, when he was engaged on the History of Brazil and increasingly interested in the treatment of Indians under Spanish and Jesuit rule.
literary_significance: The most admired of its author's later poems in his own lifetime and the one Victorian readers valued most; it is an early English Romantic example of anti-colonial sympathy expressed through the domestic romance form.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1825 in the volume containing A Vision of the Sea and other poems; the poem had been circulated in manuscript among the Lake and London circles before issue.

title: The Political Register
alternative_titles: Political Register
Weekly Political Register
description: The weekly journal founded, edited, and largely written by its author, which was the principal organ of popular radical politics in England from 1802 until his death. Its mixture of report, correspondence, pamphlet-in-serial and abuse created a new kind of political writing addressed explicitly to the mechanic and the agricultural labourer. The Register is also the vehicle in which most of its author's larger prose works, including the Rural Rides letters, first appeared.
plot_or_argument: Each number collects parliamentary and trial report, local intelligence, letters from correspondents, and a running editorial attack on what the editor calls 'the system' - paper money, sinecure, corn-law monopoly and the tax burden. In its first years the paper defended the war against Napoleon and attacked corrupt ministers; after 1812 it turned against the old officers and against Pitt's successors, and after 1815 it took up the cause of the agrarian and industrial poor. It covered Peterloo in detail, prosecuted and was prosecuted for its reports, campaigned against the six Acts, supported agitation for reform, and by the later 1820s had become the most influential single political publication in the country.
narrative_structure: Serial weekly journalism: a repeating weekly structure of report, correspondence, essay and polemic, with long runs and separate parts (the 'Pole' volumes and occasional halfpenny tax-destroys-trade numbers) gathered from the same series.
literary_form: Political journal and polemic: weekly report-and-commentary in the tradition of the eighteenth-century newspaper, transformed into an organ of extra-parliamentary agitation.
historical_context: Founded after its author's return from America and imprisonment at Bench, and stamped by the wartime fiscal state, the Corn Law of 1815, Peterloo and the long struggle over parliamentary reform; the Register survived his prosecution, the six Acts and the collapse of its earliest readership.
literary_significance: The single most important work of English radical prose of the Romantic period, and the model of a journalist's power over public opinion; E. P. Thompson made it the central evidence of a self-conscious popular political culture, and its plain idiom shaped all later plebeian journalism.
attribution_notes: Numbers are unsigned or variously signed; the overwhelming majority of the editorial matter is the founder's own, but report and correspondence in any given number may be by other hands.
bibliographical_notes: First issued weekly in January 1802 in London, and continued, with a brief interruption, until 1835; the series was gathered into annual and multi-volume 'Pole' collections bound under the same running title.

title: The Battle of Hastings; an Epic Poem in Twelve Books
description: The author's only attempt at a full-scale historical epic, twelve books of blank verse on the Norman conquest, published anonymously and almost unnoticed. Its theory of epic is austere and archaeological: the poet is to be a faithful recorder of the event, elevating nothing, inventing little, and trusting the subject itself for its terrors. The result is a strange, concentrated poem, remarkable for its hatred of the machinery of machinery and for its concentration on the physical facts of slaughter.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the death of Edward the Confessor and Harold's oath to support William's succession, then follows the Norwegian invasion of Harald Hardrada, Stamford Bridge, and the march south to Hastings. William's claim, the papal sanction, and the crossing are treated as a chain of political and legal acts rather than as providence. The central books give the battle itself in close, almost documentary detail, ending with Harold's death and the rout of the English. The later books show the submission of the English leaders and the partition of the land, closing with the Conqueror's coronation and a mournful retrospect on what England lost.
narrative_structure: Twelve books of continuous narrative with brief prefatory argument and minimal divine machinery; the action is framed by invocation and by the poet's own explicit remarks on the limits of epic invention.
principal_characters: King Harold; Duke William; King Edward the Confessor; Harald Hardrada; Earl Tostig; Odo of Bayeux
literary_form: National epic and didactic poem in the historical manner: an anti-machinal epic which treats chronicle as its authority and the battle piece as its centre.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, with a close, elided, sometimes Latinate syntax and frequent enjambment.
historical_context: Written during its author's years in Wales and Italy, and published in 1815 at the moment of Waterloo, when national epic again seemed a possible form; its austere theory of historical fidelity is a reply to the machinery of contemporary poem.
literary_significance: A significant oddity in romantic epic: it anticipates the modernist suspicion of decorative machinery, and its insistence that the poet must subordinate invention to record makes it a document of its author's classicist theory of history in verse.
attribution_notes: Published without the author's name in 1815; The book was known to its author's circle, and he accepted responsibility for it in later life, and it was admitted to his verse collections after his death.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1815, in one volume, with a prefatory dissertation on epic poetry and with the fragmentary Hymn on the Final Restoration of the Human Race appended.

title: Imaginary Conversations
alternative_titles: Imaginary Conversations of Literary Men and Statesmen
description: The author's masterpiece of prose and the first series of conversations in which two historical personages talk together about art, power, religion, and death. The dialogue form is stripped of narration: almost nothing but speech, with the characters' tempers doing the work of plot. The series ranges from Greek and Roman pairs to Italian, Spanish, and modern authors, and it established its author's reputation as the finest English prose stylist of his generation.
plot_or_argument: Each conversation places two figures in a single situation and lets their disagreement disclose character: Plato with Aristarchus on the worth of poetry, Dante with Beatrice on the price of knowledge, Pope with the Earl of Oxford, or Thrasylachus with Amycus on tyranny. There is no developing action across the volume, but within each piece pressure rises as one speaker is driven to say what he has never said before. The political conversations test whether a good man can serve a bad cause, and the literary ones argue for style as a moral rather than a decorative achievement. Recurring presences are the dignity of the private mind against public power, and the consolation of letters at the end of life.
narrative_structure: A series of self-contained prose dialogues without framing narrative, each with its own speakers, setting, and turn; the volume's unity is tonal and moral rather than sequential.
principal_characters: Plato; Aristarchus; Dante; Beatrice; Alexander; Thrasylachus; Pope; the Earl of Oxford; Joanna of Naples
literary_form: Literary dialogue and dramatic prose conversation: a Neoclassical revival of the humanist dialogue, distinguished by the absence of stage direction and by epigrammatic compression.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, in a deliberately punctilious and Latinate idiom of balanced periods and short retorts.
historical_context: Issued while its author was settled in Italy and after the Bath and Pisa years, when his quarrels with publishers and with his family had made him a professional man of letters; the series appeared while the review journals were the chief organ of literary authority, and it was received first coolly and then reverently.
literary_significance: The most important English prose style since the seventeenth-century worthies, and the origin of the modern imaginary dialogue; it shaped how later writers from Stevenson to Eliot thought about the ethics of style and the use of historical speech as argument.
bibliographical_notes: The first series was published in London in 1824 in two volumes, and a second series followed in the same year; several further series and recensions appeared through the 1820s and later, with individual conversations added, removed, and heavily revised.

title: Pericles and Aspasia; a Series of Dialogues, Letters, and Epitaphs
alternative_titles: Pericles and Aspasia
description: The author's late romance of fifth-century Athens, built up out of dialogues, letters, songs and epitaphs among Pericles, Aspasia and the intellectual society of the Periclean age. It is at once a philhellenic ideal picture and a marriage manual in classical dress, and its deliberate archaisms carry its author's prose style to its most condensed and most artificial perfection. It lies at the very end of the period covered by this installment.
plot_or_argument: The book traces Aspasia's arrival at Miletus and her influence over Pericles through the years of the Samian war, the building of the Parthenon, and the quarrels with Sparta, until the plague, the loss of friends, and the approach of the war exhaust the Periclean circle. Around the two figures move Anaxagoras, Socrates, Protagoras, Phidias, Sophocles and Thais, arguing about art, religion, and the education of women. Aspasia herself is drawn as the practical moral centre, capable of governing both a household and a statesman. The epitaphs and songs gather the civic religion of the piece, ending with the deaths of Pericles and his family.
narrative_structure: Composite prose-and-verse sequence of letters, dialogues, fragments, songs and epitaphs, arranged chronologically but without continuous narration; the reader assembles the story from documents.
principal_characters: Pericles; Aspasia; Anaxagoras; Socrates; Phidias; Sophocles
literary_form: Prose romance in epistolary and dialogue form, with lyric and funerary inscriptions; a philosophical and antiquarian fiction in the line of the author's own dialogues.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly prose, with interpolated verse songs and epitaphs in English imitations of Greek lyric and sepulchral measure.
historical_context: Composed in Bath and Florence in the last years before its author's final settlement in Italy, when Greek independence had made Hellenism a live political as well as an aesthetic question; its idealisation of Periclean Athens also answers the Reform-era debate about democracy, women's education, and the claims of art to public utility.
literary_significance: The most complete statement of its author's ideal of style as a form of moral architecture, and one of the last Victorian-adjacent English books to make classical Athens a usable model for marriage, friendship, and public taste; it sealed his late reputation with the aestheticists.
attribution_notes: Belongs to the extreme end of the Romantic period's working edges; recorded here with its date plainly stated because it postdates 1832 and overlaps the early Victorian age.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1836 in one volume, with a prefatory Advertisement; several conversations and letters were added or rewritten in later editions, including the edition of 1858.

title: A History of Brazil
alternative_titles: The History of Brazil
description: The author's great work of documentary history, the first comprehensive account in English of Portuguese Brazil from the earliest discoveries to the expulsion of the Dutch. It rests on a mass of Portuguese and Spanish printed sources and manuscript material assembled during the years of the Iberian letters and the Cid. The three volumes set out to write colonial history as a moral subject: conquest, plantation, slavery and missionary enterprise are all weighed and judged.
plot_or_argument: The first volume narrates the discovery and the plantation of the coast, the captaincy system, and the long war with the French interlopers, with a substantial natural history of the country. The second covers the Dutch invasion and the quarter-century of Nassau's rule in Pernambuco, the sugar economy, and the religious and racial politics of the colony. The third brings the story to the restoration of Portuguese authority and to the mature colonial society of the eighteenth century. Throughout the author documents the treatment of the Indians, the Jesuit missions, and the slave trade, and repeatedly condemns the avarice of settlers and administrators.
narrative_structure: Formal annalistic history in three volumes, chronological and documentary, with long digressive chapters on natural history, ethnography, and colonial administration and heavy citation of printed sources in the notes.
literary_form: National and colonial history on the model of Robertson, with an antiquarian's apparatus and a moralist's commentary.
historical_context: Published while the Peninsular War made Portugal a British ally and while the Brazilian court had removed to Rio de Janeiro, so that its subject was a matter of current imperial policy; its abolitionist passages answer the campaigns of the same decade.
literary_significance: The standard English history of colonial Brazil for most of the nineteenth century and a major document of romantic-era imperial scholarship, evidencing how a poet of the Lyrical Ballads generation became an archivist of the Atlantic world; its treatment of slavery and of the Indians is central to the period's moral debate on empire.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in three volumes appearing in succession from 1810, with maps and engravings, and reprinted in a second edition later; the first volume appeared in 1810 and the completion of the work was long delayed by its author's other researches.

title: The Life of our Rev. John Wesley
alternative_titles: The Life of the Rev. John Wesley
Life of Wesley
description: The author's two-volume biography of the Methodist founder, compiled largely from Wesley's own journals and letters and from documents supplied to him by the Methodist leadership. It presents Wesley as a providential restorer of vital religion in England while insisting that his connexions were schismatic and should be dissolved. The book was a publishing event and an offence, and the quarrel it provoked with the Methodist preachers occupied its author for several years.
plot_or_argument: The narrative follows Wesley from Epworth and Oxford through the Georgia voyage and the Aldersgate experience to the open-air preaching, the building of the connexional system, and the last years. The biographer stresses Wesley's learning, his industry, and his political quietism, and treats the revival as a divine visitation to a slothful church. At the same time he argues that the Methodist itinerants and their chapels are an illegal and unnecessary separation, and that after Wesley's death union with the established church is the duty of Methodists. The volumes reprint long passages of the Journal, of letters, and of doctrinal tracts, annotated critically, so that Wesley's own voice is permitted to answer his critics.
narrative_structure: Chronological biography interwoven with extensive quotation from the subject's own journals and correspondence, and with argumentative notes and appendices; narrative and polemic alternate by design.
principal_characters: John Wesley; Charles Wesley; George Whitefield; the Methodist preachers of the connexion
literary_form: Prose biography and religious history with documentary appendix, in the evangelical life-writing tradition, turned to a church-political argument.
historical_context: Written when Methodism was negotiating its legal separation from the Church of England and when its author was consolidating his position as a church-and-state writer after the laureateship; it drew replies, pamphlet wars, and a defence in the Quarterly Review, and its text was revised in later editions as the quarrel continued.
literary_significance: The earliest scholarly biography of Wesley and a primary source for the Methodist journal, whose editorial practice - reprinting and commenting on the subject's own papers - made it a model and a warning for later religious biography; it is essential evidence of the romantic-era relation between revival and established religion.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in two volumes, with a second edition and later reprints revised in response to the Methodist controversy over the biographer's account of Wesley's ordinations.

title: The History of the Peninsular War
alternative_titles: History of the Peninsular War, which invaded Portugal in 1807
description: The author's monumental narrative of the war in Spain and Portugal, written from official despatches, Portuguese and Spanish sources, and the testimony of officers he interviewed at first hand. It is at once a campaign history, a defence of the Spanish and Portuguese peoples, and a partisan account of British conduct of the war. As laureate and as an old Iberian traveller, its author made the subject his own.
plot_or_argument: The work begins with Junot's march into Portugal in 1807 and the convention of Cintra, and follows the war through Moore's retreat, Wellington's campaigns, the Sieges of Badajoz and Ciudad Rodrigo, Salamanca, Vitoria and the Pyrenees. It gives equal space to the guerrilla and to the popular rising of 1808, insisting that the peninsula's own resistance, not British generalship alone, wore the French down. It also weighs the politics of the Cortes of Cadiz, the regency, and the restored Ferdinand VII, whose treatment of his liberators the historian records with bitterness. The final volumes carry the narrative to the close of the war and the French expedition of 1823, with copious notes on sources and on disputed dates.
narrative_structure: Multi-volume chronological campaign history with substantial notes, appendices of despatches and returns, and recurring interpretive chapters on Spanish and Portuguese politics.
literary_form: Military and political history in the narrative manner of the period, combining official-document editing with eyewitness inquiry.
historical_context: Written in the long peace after Waterloo, when the Peninsular War was being absorbed into national memory and into Wellington's monument, and when the Holy Alliance's intervention in Spain in 1823 made the recent past an immediate political issue.
literary_significance: The authoritative English account of the Peninsular War for a generation and a key text of romantic-era nationalism and liberal sympathy for Spain; it also documents how a poet of the 1790s turned the historical method he had learned in Brazil against the diplomacy of the Restoration.
bibliographical_notes: Published in successive volumes in London between 1823 and the early 1830s, with maps and plans, and reissued in a cheaper library edition; the last volume was delayed by its author's other labours and by his disputes with fellow writers on the subject.

title: Omniana
alternative_titles: Omniana; or, Results and Suggestions of Literature, and of Opinions in Politics, Economics, and Religion
description: A two-volume miscellany of anecdotes, quotations, and short disquisitions on literature, politics, economy and religion, gathered from commonplace books and printed out of a professed indifference to system. Its manner - erudite, Tory, sententious, and full of unacknowledged quotation - is that of the author of Letters from England, and it was published anonymously. It is the least-annotated of its author's prose works and the one whose authorship is least settled.
plot_or_argument: The items pass from Elizabethan drama and forgotten pamphlets to the corn trade, the poor laws, and the practice of abstracting books, with long transcriptions from scarce writers. Political entries defend prescription, order, and the settled constitution, and attack the speculators and paper-mongers of the war years. Several pieces argue for a national literature governed by the church and the universities. The miscellany closes on moral and religious reflection, with the compiler's own opinion always withheld or delivered in another's words.
narrative_structure: Miscellany of numbered items of very unequal length with no arrangement by subject; the reader's sequence is that of the compiler's commonplace book rather than an argument.
literary_form: Literary miscellany and commonplace-book prose: anecdote, quotation and short essay after the manner of the eighteenth-century analecta.
historical_context: Compiled in the war years of high prices and paper currency, when its author was consolidating his editorial and antijacobin career and contributing to the Quarterly Review; its Tory economics and its antiquarian reading answer the period's expansion of literary history and periodical culture.
literary_significance: It preserves much rare material from books now hard to trace and is a document of the romantic-era habit of quotation; its editorship also bears on the dating and authentication of several short poems and sayings otherwise unrecorded.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in 1812 and attributed on the strength of publisher's accounts and contemporary evidence; the share of a collaborating friend has been raised in the bibliographical literature, so the attribution to a single author is not universally conceded, and part of the compilation may be by another hand.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1812 in two volumes, anonymously, and reprinted afterwards among its author's prose works under his own name.

title: Rural Rides
alternative_titles: Rural Rides, in the years 1821, 1822, &c., with Letters on the Times
description: The author's pedestrian and hack rides through southern, midland and northern England, and into Wales, written up as letters for the Political Register and gathered into a book in 1830. This record describes the book form of 1830, which reprinted the serial letters and added the Letters on the Times. The rides turn topography into political argument: every hedgerow, turnpike and workhouse is read as evidence of the condition of agriculture and of the labourer.
plot_or_argument: The rides follow roads from Berkshire and Hampshire into Wiltshire, the midland counties, and the north, and from North Wales across the border counties, revisiting places seen decades earlier. At each stage the writer reports fares at public houses, wages, the state of the enclosures, the roads, the tithe, and the aspect of the villages, and compares what he sees with what he remembers. The argument throughout is that the paper system, the taxes, and the corn laws have impoverished a country formerly prosperous, and that the labourer's table is now bare where it once was full. The later letters add a polemic against the clergy, against the poor-law officers, and against the 'distance' and 'fine feelings' of the rich.
narrative_structure: Serial letters of travel, reordered and enlarged in book form; each ride is a self-contained route narrative with appended letters of general argument, and the whole is organised geographically and retrospectively rather than by a single thesis.
literary_form: Topographical and travel prose in epistolary form, a pedestrian tour transformed into political economy and social survey.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, in a colloquial, Anglo-Saxon idiom built on concrete nouns, direct address and invective.
historical_context: Conducted and written between post-war depression, the Six Acts, the repeal of the Corn Law agitation and the Reform crisis, with the rides of 1821-22 answering the agricultural distress after 1815 and the later rides answering Catholic emancipation and the vote reform debates.
literary_significance: The founding text of English social survey in literary form, and the witness on which all later accounts of the romantic-era rural labourer depend; it made the road narrative an instrument of class analysis and remains the most quoted prose of English radicalism.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in the Political Register from 1821 through the early 1830s and first collected in book form in 1830 from the Political Register Office, with later editions enlarged to include the rides of the last years; this record describes the 1830 collected issue.

title: A History of the Protestant "Reformation" in England and Ireland
alternative_titles: History of the Protestant Reformation in England and Ireland
description: The author's polemic history of the English and Irish Reformation, issued in parts and in two volumes, which reads the dissolution of the monasteries as the origin of the modern confiscation of the poor. Its notorious device is the scare quotes around 'Reformation', a word the author uses to mean robbery dressed in Protestant language. The book is at once a work of documentary history and the most sustained religious attack of his later career.
plot_or_argument: The narrative begins with the state of religion and learning before the break with Rome, and then documents the visitations, the surrenders, and the partition of monastic lands among the new purchasers. It argues that the Reformation's real business was the extinction of the hospitals, alms, and schools maintained out of church property, and that the poorer classes were made destitute at the same stroke. Irish chapters carry the argument further, treating the plantations and the persecution of the Irish peasantry as the same confiscation applied to another people. Throughout, the historian quotes the reformers themselves, especially Foxe, to make them witnesses against their own cause.
narrative_structure: Chronological documentary history in two volumes, with long verbatim extracts from primers, chronicles, acts of parliament and Foxe's Acts and Monuments, framed by an uninterrupted editorial harangue.
principal_characters: Henry the Eighth; Thomas Cromwell; Archbishop Cranmer; Queen Elizabeth; the monks and abbots of the dissolved houses; the Irish of the plantations
literary_form: Polemic ecclesiastical history and controversy, in the tradition of Reformation and counter-Reformation writing turned to a radical agrarian argument.
historical_context: Written in the aftermath of the Corn Law depression and on the eve of the Irish and Reform agitations, when the property of the dissolved monasteries and the tithe were live legislative questions; the book's attack on the church-endowed state helped make its author a hostile figure to the moderate reformers.
literary_significance: The most influential nineteenth-century popular account of the Reformation as an act of class confiscation, and a primary document in the history of the Catholic-and-radical reading of English religion; it fixed the phrase 'the Protestant Reformation' in its ironic modern use.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in parts and then in two volumes between 1824 and 1826 from the Political Register Office, and reprinted many times, the earlier numbers being bound under the running title of the Register; frequently reissued under the shortened title with the quotation marks retained.

title: A Grammar of the English Language
alternative_titles: Grammar of the English Language
description: The author's grammar, first written for his son at school in America and then issued as a book for the English labouring classes. It teaches parts of speech, syntax, prosody and composition through sentences drawn from ordinary speech and from the best writers, and it is candidly polemical against Latin and French derived rules. The volume also carries his famous account of the 'Saxon' idiom and his insistence that clear writing is a moral as well as a civic accomplishment.
plot_or_argument: The rules are set out in question-and-answer form, with parsing exercises on sentences of farm, shop and workshop, and with corrections of faulty examples. The writer argues that English is a language of short Saxon words which should be preferred to long derived ones, and that the grammar of the tongue is learned by use and imitation rather than by translation from Latin. He gives instructions on spelling, on the choice of words, and on writing plain prose, and adds advice on reading the best English authors. The later part addresses composition, punctuation and versification, and argues that a labourer's child properly taught has the same access to the language as a gentleman's.
narrative_structure: Didactic treatise in progressive lessons with exercises and examples, addressed in a first-person voice to a pupil and to his parent; prefaced by an account of the book's origin in correspondence with the author's son.
literary_form: Grammar and didactic prose, a schoolbook consciously written as an instrument of popular education rather than as scholarship.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, with illustrative verse passages on prosody.
historical_context: Written after its author's American exile and his son's schooling at Bristol, and issued cheaply as part of the series of useful knowledge for mechanics and labourers that flourished in the later 1810s alongside the Lancasterian schools and the mechanics' institutes.
literary_significance: One of the most widely read English grammar books of the nineteenth century, long a standard school text in Britain and America, and a key document of the period's belief that control of the standard language was a route to political enfranchisement.
bibliographical_notes: First issued in book form in 1819, having been prepared earlier for private use and published as part of a cheap series of useful works; it went through many editions and enlargements, and was reprinted after his death with editorial alterations.

title: Advice to Young Men
alternative_titles: Advice to Young Men, and (Incidentally) to Old Men
Advice to Young Men, and (incidentally) to Old Men, in the middle and in advanced life
description: The author's book of conduct for the young man of the labouring and trading classes, addressed from the experience of a self-made farmer and journalist. It covers drink, tobacco, dress, duelling, gambling, love, marriage, and the choice of a trade, with a long and famous section on marriage and on the government of a household. Its tone is paternal, blunt, and combatively anti-genteel, and its economics are those of independence and of the small proprietor.
plot_or_argument: The young man is warned first against gin and against tobacco, which are presented as taxes on his health and his wages as well as vices. He is told to keep clear of the military, of the law, and of the church as professions, and to learn something with his hands; to dress plainly, to avoid the theatre and the racecourse, and to save. On marriage he is advised to marry for competence and character rather than for beauty or fortune, to court shortly and openly, and to keep a household that owes nothing. The incidental advice to old men rebukes them for having set the example the young are asked to refuse, and the book ends on the duties of a father and of an English yeoman.
narrative_structure: Epistolary and hortatory prose running through a graded set of subjects, with anecdotes of the author's own life and occasional apostrophes to the reader; no plot, but a single sustained address.
literary_form: Conduct book and familiar essay in the tradition of the domestic and economical treatise, rewritten as popular radical instruction.
historical_context: Published in the year of Catholic emancipation and of the onset of the Reform agitation, when its author was reworking his image as a father of the people; it draws on his own American and English farming experience and on the conduct literature he had always quoted against his opponents.
literary_significance: The most durable of its author's non-polemical books and a standard work of nineteenth-century popular self-help, influential on both sides of the Atlantic as a manual of plebeian respectability; it is central evidence of the moral language of English radicalism.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1829 from the Political Register Office, in one volume, and reprinted repeatedly through the nineteenth century, including cheap and abridged editions and an edition prepared after his death.

title: A Paper Against Gold
alternative_titles: Paper Against Gold
description: The author's great currency pamphlet, made out of the letters on paper credit which had appeared in the Political Register during and after the Restriction period. It argues that paper money and the national debt together transfer the substance of the country from producers to fundholders, and that the return to cash payments would restore honest measure. The book is the clearest statement of his 'distance' theory of political economy and the most quoted of his economic writing.
plot_or_argument: The letters define gold and paper as measures of value and show how a debased measure raises nominal prices while lowering the real reward of labour. They trace the national debt from its origins in the funds to the sinking-fund and tax machinery that served it, and name the classes that gained by the system: contractors, jobbers, and the great monied interest. The post-war depression, the fall of agricultural prices and the distress of 1815-16 are offered as proof that the system works against the producer. The remedy proposed is a return to coin, the reduction of the debt and of the civil and military establishments, and the repeal of the corn laws, with an appeal to the labourer to understand the mechanism that robs him.
narrative_structure: A sequence of numbered letters forming a continuous argument, written for the Register and gathered into a single pamphlet volume, with the reasoning advancing from definition to history to remedy.
literary_form: Political economy and commercial writing in the form of open letters and polemic pamphlet.
historical_context: Written at the moment of the resumption of cash payments and the agricultural distress after Waterloo, in the same debate that produced the Bullion Report and the Corn Law of 1815; it gave the currency argument a popular vocabulary and cost its author much of his earlier supporting readership.
literary_significance: The most influential popular exposition of the case against paper credit and the funded debt in the period, and a source for all later radical-economic accounts of the transition from a Saxon to a moneyed England; E. P. Thompson treated it as the hinge of its author's conversion to the labouring poor.
bibliographical_notes: First issued in pamphlet form in 1816, gathered from letters previously printed in the Political Register in 1815 and 1816, and reprinted several times, sometimes bound with the following currency letters.

title: Rose Aylmer
description: The author's shortest and most celebrated lyric, a quiet elegy for a girl of his childhood neighbourhood who died abroad. Twenty-four lines of plain, monosyllabic diction recall a shared village schooling and a wood fire seen at a distance, and then pass to the news of her death and to the poet's wakeful remembrance. It is the poem by which its author enters the anthologies, and its extreme spareness is quite unlike the texture of Gebir or the dialogues.
plot_or_argument: The speaker and Rose Aylmer grew up together in the same village, rang the same bell, and learned the same lesson; he saw her mostly at a distance, by the blaze he set in the chinks of the turpentine bark at nightfall, and shouted to her among the birds. Years later they met again, and she sailed away to India, where the poem reports that she died. The closing movement gathers the tokens of her affection - the broken ring, the ring's divided half, the dying gift - and ends by consecrating to her memory a night of recollection and sighs which her living eyes could not be present to.
narrative_structure: A single brief lyric moving from the shared childhood scene to the distant fire, to separation and reported death, and closing in an address to the dead; the argument is carried by a sequence of remembered images rather than by events.
literary_form: Short elegiac lyric and epitaphic poem of mourning for a private friend; a romantic revival of the simple elegy on the model of the ballad stanza and of Ben Jonson's lyric.
meter_and_prosody: Short accentual lines alternating four-beat and three-beat movement, with an irregular rhyme; the monosyllabic diction and the epigrammatic close give the stanza an epitaphic weight.
historical_context: Composed in the later 1790s, when its author was an undergraduate at Oxford and estranged from his family; Rose Aylmer, an Anglo-Indian he had known in childhood, died in India around 1800, and the poem's revised stanzas carry that news. It belongs to the decade's revival of the unadorned elegy.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised short poems of the romantic period and the locus classicus of its author's reputation as a lyricist, its praise of monosyllabic plainness became a touchstone for later arguments about style, memory and the elegy for an ordinary friend.
attribution_notes: The usual dating of composition is the later 1790s, with revision after the news of Rose Aylmer's death abroad, and the poem was first printed some years after it was written; the composition-to-publication gap is long and the earlier versions are known only from manuscript and from later reprint. Scholarly accounts give the first appearance as 1806, but the venue of that first printing is not settled, and the author himself reprinted and revised the poem in later collections.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1806 according to the standard bibliographical accounts, and afterwards reprinted, with revisions, in its author's later verse collections and in the collected editions of his works.

title: Specimens of the Later English Poets, with Preliminary Notices
alternative_titles: Specimens of the Later English Poets, in Three Volumes
description: The author's anthology of modern English verse, planned as a companion to the collections of specimens of the earlier English poets and issued in three volumes with substantial preliminary notices on each poet. The selection is wide and deliberate, rescuing minor and forgotten writers while judging the famous, and the notices are essays in criticism rather than mere biography. It is the best document we have of how a laureate-in-waiting read the poetry of the previous half-century.
plot_or_argument: The volumes arrange extracts from poets writing since the middle of the eighteenth century, each preceded by a notice of the writer's life, character, and principal works, and followed by comments on particular poems. The editor praises Cowper's originality and faults his religious melancholy, gives an early and influential estimate of Robert Burns, and appraises the descriptive, topographical, and sentimental schools. He sets the doctrine of a national poetry against mere delicacy, and argues for seriousness of subject, for the dignity of the labouring writer, and for the critic's duty to the reader rather than to the party. The collection also prints much verse otherwise hard to trace, from odes and sonnets to ballads and local poems.
narrative_structure: Anthology organised by author, each unit consisting of a biographical and critical notice followed by selected extracts; there is no continuous argument across volumes, though the notices accumulate a critical position.
literary_form: Editorial anthology with prefatory critical commentary: a specimens collection in the line of the Reliques and of the earlier English specimens, used as a vehicle for review-style criticism.
meter_and_prosody: Prose notices framing verse extracts of every kind.
historical_context: Compiled when the successful sale of earlier specimens collections had made literary antiquarianism a market, and when the review journals were establishing professional criticism; it belongs to the years in which its author was moving from radical verse to editorial and critical authority.
literary_significance: A primary source for the period's canon-formation and for the earliest critical estimates of Burns and Cowper, and a document of the transition of the poet into the editor-critic; its notices are still quarried for evidence on eighteenth-century and romantic reputation.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1807 in three volumes by Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, the venture proposed as a companion to the successful specimens of the earlier English poets then in print.

title: Sir Thomas More; or, Colloquies on the Progress and Prospects of Society
alternative_titles: Sir Thomas More, a Colloquy
description: The author's late prose colloquy, long gestating and issued in two volumes, in which the writer converses with the ghost or the spirit of Sir Thomas More about the condition and the future of society. It is the most systematic of his prose works, ranging over education, the press, the working classes, pauperism, Rome, and the colonies in a humanist dialogue form. The book is a storehouse of the period's anxieties about progress, and was later quarried by Marx for its evidence on the manufacturing system.
plot_or_argument: More, learned and sceptical, is made to survey the modern world from the vantage of a man who knew another civilisation before the Reformation and the age of commerce. He questions the writer about the diffusion of knowledge through cheap print, about the education of the poorer classes, and about whether the increase of reading has improved the readers. Other colloquies treat the condition of labour, the growth of the towns, the state of Ireland, Roman Catholic claims, the colonies and slavery, and the prospects of Christianity in an age of machinery and of political change. The argument throughout is conservative in method but genuinely alarmed: material progress is admitted, and then weighed against the moral and religious cost, with More pressing toward a defence of counsel, conscience, and settled order.
narrative_structure: Series of colloquies in dialogue form between the author and the shade of More, without dramatic setting or plot; each colloquy takes up one subject and is free to digress into report, history, and prophecy.
principal_characters: Sir Thomas More; the enquiring writer
literary_form: Humanist dialogue and moral-philosophical prose, a Christian-humanist colloquy of the kind written by More himself, turned to the question of social progress.
historical_context: Published in the years of post-war depression, of the quarrel over Catholic emancipation, and of the first factory and education legislation; the first volume appeared in 1829, on the eve of the Reform crisis, and the second followed soon after, when the debate about the 'condition of England' was opening.
literary_significance: The most complete statement of its author's social thought and one of the most quoted conservative analyses of the manufacturing age, important both as a document of romantic-era Toryism and as a source of evidence on early industrial conditions later used by writers of the opposite opinion.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in two volumes, the first in 1829 and the second soon after, by the author's regular publisher of these years; long in preparation from the later 1810s, and reprinted in a cheaper edition during the century.

title: The Life of William Cowper, Esq.
alternative_titles: The Life of Cowper
Letters of the Rev. William Cowper
description: The author's biography of William Cowper, written as the life prefacing a collected edition of Cowper's works and built on the poet's correspondence and on interviews with survivors. It is a work of editorial as much as of narrative art, and its frank handling of Cowper's madness and of his religious terror made it the most discussed English literary biography of the later 1830s. Its use of private letters also set a precedent, and a warning, for the practice of literary biography.
plot_or_argument: The Life narrates Cowper's school years, his apprenticeship and his first poetry, the friendship with Lady Austen and the years at Olney, the partnership with Mrs. Unwin, and the later settlement at East Dereham and Weston Underwood. It prints and comments on the correspondence with the Rev. Mr. Newton, and gives a clinical and unsentimental account of the poet's depressions, his attempted suicide, and his final evangelical assurance. The biographer draws from the letters a picture of rural and manufacturing England, including Cowper's own condemnation of the way poor parents bound out and ruined their children. The publication of certain letters gave offence to surviving friends and relatives, who objected to what had been made public.
narrative_structure: Chronological literary biography interwoven with long quoted correspondence and with documentary extract; narrative, letters, and editorial comment alternate, with topographical and social matter folded into the record of the life.
principal_characters: William Cowper; the Rev. Mr. Newton; Mrs. Unwin; Lady Austen; Mrs. Connard; the curate of Olney
literary_form: Prose biography and edited correspondence: a life prefacing collected works, in the evangelical memoir tradition but practised as literary history.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, quoting verse and letters at length.
historical_context: Prepared after its author had obtained access to Cowper's papers from the surviving collaterals, and issued in a cheap collected edition of the works in the mid 1830s; the controversy over its use of private letters ran for years and drew replies from those who thought the family betrayed.
literary_significance: The foundation of all later Cowper scholarship and a decisive text in the history of literary biography and of editorial ethics; its documentary passages on eighteenth-century labour and the manufacturing system have been used as social evidence by writers of every politics since.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1835 as the Life prefacing a collected edition of Cowper's works issued in London in that year and completing in the later 1830s, with the correspondence edited by its author from the original letters in the family's hands.

title: A Parliamentary History of England, from the earliest Period to the Year 1803
alternative_titles: Parliamentary History of England, from the earliest period to the year 1803
Parliamentary History and Debates
description: The author's great publishing enterprise: a cheap complete record of English parliaments, from the earliest period to 1803, continued by the Debates of his own time, issued in parts and gathered into thirty-six volumes. It was a working man's edition of the constitution, putting the record of what parliaments had said and done within reach of the reading public. Its author used it to supply the documentary basis for his own history of taxation, monopoly, and corruption.
plot_or_argument: The series reprints and continues the earlier collections of parliamentary history and state trials, adds the debates of the reigns from George the First onwards, and covers the sessions of the author's own day. It records the business of the two houses, the petitions and the remonstrances, and the division lobbies, with editorial prefaces that interpret the record for the reader. The editor's purpose is polemical as well as archival: to show by documents how the revolution of property, the funding system, and the corruption of the representation had been legislated into existence, and to give the labouring reader evidence he can use for himself.
narrative_structure: Multi-volume serial compilation arranged by parliament and by session, with prefatory and connecting editorial matter; the order of the record is chronological, and the argument emerges cumulatively across the whole.
literary_form: Documentary compilation and record of parliamentary proceedings, with editorial history and polemic; a reference work built as an instrument of popular politics.
historical_context: Begun in the years after the Act of Union and the failure of parliamentary reform, and issued in weekly and monthly parts at prices deliberately set for mechanics and farm labourers; the enterprise was also a commercial and personal quarrel, since others claimed the labour of its composition.
literary_significance: The standard cheap repository of parliamentary record for the nineteenth century and still a cited source for debates not otherwise reported, and the material foundation of its author's whole political economy of the 'system'; it made documentary evidence a popular possession.
attribution_notes: The series reprints and continues earlier collections, and the question of how much of the composition was done by others, and under whose claim, was disputed in its author's lifetime and since; it is recorded here as his publication and editorial undertaking.
bibliographical_notes: First numbers issued in 1806, and the work completed in thirty-six volumes in London between 1806 and 1820, printed in parts and in double-column folio-style pages, the later volumes carrying the Debates to the close of the 1810s.
